title: RFC 2693 -- SPKI certificate theory structures (DERIVED)
$comment: DERIVED -- not verbatim. RFC 2693 ships NO formal grammar of any kind: no ABNF, ASN.1, CDDL, JSON Schema or BNF. Its Abstract says why: 'This document gives the theory behind SPKI certificates and ACLs without going into technical detail about those structures or their uses.' Every keyword in this file was written for this record and must never be quoted as RFC 2693's own schema. The source passages each entry rests on are held byte-exact in the five *.verbatim.txt files beside this one and are cited here by region id. ||| DERIVED FROM: RFC 2693, 'SPKI Certificate Theory', Ellison/Frantz/Lampson/Rivest/Thomas/Ylonen, September 1999, Experimental, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2693.txt>, source sha256 6822d668195c3d9b391f0c4f2b023341ba0e5a72e59d63c366a520de42c99098. Sections 1.1, 2.6.1-2.10, 3.4, 4.1.4, 5-5.6, 5.7.2, 6-6.5.7, 7, 7.3, 7.5, 7.7. ||| TWO LEVELS. (1) The S-expression forms the source prints -- name, hash, tag and the *-forms, k-of-n, (null) -- modelled as JSON under the MAPPING below. (2) The abstract records the source defines by enumerating elements but never encodes -- the 5-tuple, the 4-tuple, validity, the online tests and the instruments they fetch, the certificate bodies, the ACL entry. Their JSON shape (array positions, member names) is this project's rendering of the enumerated elements. The concrete S-expression structure of those records is the business of 'the SPKI structure definition' (Section 5.7.2) -- draft-ietf-spki-cert-structure, a separate record -- and nothing here is imported from it. ||| MAPPING (PROJECT CONVENTION, not from RFC 2693): an S-expression list maps to a JSON array of its elements, in order; an octet string (the source's byte string) maps to a JSON string of the same length whose i-th character is the code point equal to the i-th octet, U+0000-U+00FF (ISO-8859-1 decoding). So printable-ASCII atoms map to themselves, #03# maps to the one-character string U+0003, and |TLCgPLFlGTzgUbcaYLW8kGTEnUk=| maps to a 20-character string. This is a bijection between S-expressions without display hints and JSON values built from strings (every character at most U+00FF) and non-empty arrays that begin with a string. The source never prints a display hint, so none is mapped. ||| STATUS. Every $defs entry carries x-status: 'derived' (encodes a definition or template the source states), 'derived-from-example' (encodes the shape of printed examples; no template is printed), 'inferred' (not literally stated; the $comment gives the reasoning), 'opaque' (the source says the thing exists but gives it no form), or 'project-convention'. An entry whose x-status is not 'inferred' but which rests partly on an inference or a project choice lists each such keyword in x-inferred, so no inference is marked only in prose. Every entry also carries x-quotes: the source text it encodes, with section, line range and verbatim region id. Quotes are verbatim modulo line-wrapping -- each run of whitespace in the source, including a line break and the next line's indent, is one space -- so a word the source hyphenates across a line break appears as e.g. 'LISP- like'. No quote crosses a page break; a sentence that does is quoted in two parts. x-status, x-inferred, x-quotes, x-constraints, x-gaps and x-requirements are annotation keywords: validators ignore them. Each x-constraints and x-gaps item names, in x-requirements, the rfc-2693#R-NNNN entries of requirements.yaml it rests on (added by the cross-check pass). ||| OPEN AND CLOSED. Tuples and tuple validity are closed, because Sections 6.1 and 6.2 enumerate their elements ('The elements of a 5-tuple are:'). Every other record is open, because the source states minimum content only ('It contains at least an Issuer and a Subject', 'a request containing a nonce') and says it omits technical detail. ||| ROOT. The root is the 5-tuple, the central structure (Section 6.1). Validate anything else against its own $defs entry by reference, e.g. {"$ref": "spki-theory.derived.schema.json#/$defs/tag"}. ||| WHAT NO KEYWORD HERE CAN CHECK is collected under $defs/NOT-EXPRESSIBLE (x-constraints SC-01..SC-19, x-gaps G-01..G-16). Read it before trusting a green result. ||| $id is a placeholder, as in rfc-8785's derived schema, pending a decision on whether this library publishes schema identifiers.

byte-string.$comment: An S-expression atom. The source calls it a byte string (Sections 2.7, 2.8, 6.2, 6.3.1) and, in the glossary, a string. Rendered as a JSON string under the octet-to-code-point MAPPING of the root $comment; the pattern admits exactly the characters U+0000-U+00FF, i.e. exactly the images of octet strings. The source sets no length bound. It also draws a distinction this file keeps: Section 6.3.1 sets 'S-expressions' beside 'byte-strings', so here an s-expression is a list, a byte-string an atom, and a sexp-item either. The canonical form the Abstract mentions is not defined in this source (it is RFC 9804's subject; see that record).

x-quotes.text: S-EXPRESSION: the data format chosen for SPKI/SDSI. This is a LISP- like parenthesized expression with the limitations that empty lists are not allowed and the first element in any S-expression must be a string, called the "type" of the expression.

s-expression.$comment: A list. 'empty lists are not allowed' is minItems 1; the first element must be a string, which is the first prefixItems entry. Later elements are byte strings or lists. The type element is the discriminator every printed form uses: name, hash, k-of-n, null, tag, *.

x-quotes.text: An authorization is a list of strings or sub-lists

x-quotes.text: PRINCIPAL: a cryptographic key, capable of generating a digital signature. We deal with public-key signatures in this document but any digital signature method should apply.

The private key must be kept secret, so it is not a possible identifier, but each public key corresponds to one private key and therefore to one keyholder. The public key, viewed as a byte string, is therefore an identifier for the keyholder.
We use S-expressions as the standard format for these certificates and define a canonical form for those S-expressions.
That is, the keys in a threshold subject do not need to have the same algorithm.

public-key.$comment: OPAQUE CONTENT, INFERRED SHAPE. The source never prints a public key: keys appear only as symbols (K1, K2, Kroot, Ki, <root key>), and no algorithm, encoding or field is given. Two inferences are made here and both are flagged. (1) A key is an S-expression list -- from the Abstract's statement that S-expressions are the format. (2) Its type is none of the type names this source gives its own forms (name, hash, k-of-n, null, tag, *). Neither is stated. They are made so the printed forms stay disjoint, and every concrete example agrees with them: each fully qualified name the source prints carries a list (a hash) in position 2, no relative name does, and the reserved word Self (Section 6.1) is a byte string. WITHOUT them -- if a key may be a bare byte string, as Section 2.7's 'viewed as a byte string' could be read -- (name fred sam) is ambiguous between a relative name and a key followed by one name, Self is ambiguous with a key, and any S-expression at all would satisfy subject as a key, so no subject could ever be rejected. Section 7.7: keys within one threshold subject need not share an algorithm, so nothing here ties one key's form to another's (gap G-10).

If on-line tests are involved in the certificate processing, then the validity dates of those on-line test results are intersected by VIntersect() [defined in 6.3.2, below] with the validity dates of the certificate to yield the dates in the certificate's tuple(s).
